headline: Welcome to the live coverage of stage 21 of La Vuelta 26
subtext: It’s the end of the road. After over 3,000 kilometres of racing, with some 5,000 metres of elevation gain, from Monaco, home to the Salida Official of La Vuelta 26 three weeks ago, the peloton are in Granada for the final stage. It will be an exilarating finale, with a punchy circuit around the iconic Alhambra to cap off this 81st edition. The times for the general classification will be neutralised as the riders pass the finish line for the penultimate time (9.8 km to go). There won’t be time bonuses at the finish. The neutral start from Carrefour Granada is set at 16:20, the start proper at 16:23 after a 1.1 km parade, and the winners should be crowned at around 19:15.

headline: A historic finale
subtext: In its 81st edition, La Vuelta finishes in Granada for the first time. Madrid is the venue that has crowned the final winners on most occasions (55), ahead of Bilbao (13), San Sebastián (6), Santiago de Compostela (3), and then Miranda de Ebro, Salamanca and Jerez de la Frontera (1 each). Granada was a stage town already in the first La Vuelta (1935), and it hosted the Gran Salida in 2005 and 2008. The iconic Alhambra was visited by La Vuelta in 1974, 1975 and 2005. The last stage winner in Granada is Adam Yates two years ago. Granada has hosted many other cycling events, including Spain’s national road championships last year. Ivan Romeo won the men elite ITT. Jack Haig won stage 4 of the 2020 Vuelta a Andalucia in Granada.

headline: Remembering the Galera brothers
subtext: Today’s start from Carrefour Granada sees the riders roll from Armilla, the hometown of the Galera brothers. Born in 1940, Joaquin Galera won a stage of the Tour de France in 1965 and passed away last year. His younger brother Manuel was born in 1943 and died after a crash during the 1972 edition of the Vuelta a Andalucia. The same year, the Memorial Manuel Galera was celebrated for the first time. 33 editions were held until 2004. Among the winners of the Memorial Manuel Galera, Francis Cabello hails from La Zubia (km 18 on today’s route). He participated in 11 editions of La Vuelta between 1990 and 2004 and won a Tour de France stage in 1994.

headline: La Roja
subtext: The all-out action en route to Collado del Alguacil all but settled the overall battle. Enric Mas (Movistar) is set to become the 64th different overall winner of La Vuelta. He will be the 25th different Spanish winner of La Vuelta, the first since Alberto Contador in 2014.It will also be the fifth La Vuelta overall victory in the history of team Movistar after the successes of Pedro Delgado (1989, under the sponsorship of Reynolds), Abraham Olano (1998, Banesto), Alejandro Valverde (2009, Caisse d’Épargne), and Nairo Quintana (2016, Movistar). Primoz Roglic is set to stand on the podium of La Vuelta for the 6th time: winner in 2019, 2020, 2021, and 2024; second in 2026; third in 2023. He matches Roberto Heras' record. Only Alejandro Valverde has more La Vuelta GC top 3 results: 7. Behind them, Enric Mas is up to 5, like Pedro Delgado and Luis Ocaña. Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) is set to be the first Austrian podium finisher in La Vuelta. The best result achieved so far by one of his compatriots was 5th place by Max Bulla in 1935 (the first edition).

headline: Green jersey
subtext: Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike) is set to become the 13th Belgian winner of the points standings of La Vuelta, the second this century after Greg Van Avermaet in 2008. It will be his second victory in a Grand Tour standings, after the points classification of the Tour de France 2022. After his breakaway yesterday, Van Aert has 326 points, 87 more than his Visma-Lease a Bike teammate Matthew Brennan. Alessandro Romele (XDS Astana) completes the top 3 with 171 points. There are 50 points up for grabs today: 20 at the intermediate sprint and 30 at the finish.

headline: Polka dot jersey
subtext: Despite Wout van Aert’s assault yesterday, Santiago Buitrago (Bahrain Victorious) is set to become the fifth Colombian winner of the mountains standings of La Vuelta after Luis Herrera (1987, 1991), Oscar de Jesus Vargas (1989), Martin Farfan (1990) and Felix Cardenas (2003, 2004). With his many attacks in the mountains, Buitrago claimed 78 points, 16 more than Van Aert. Andreas Leknessund (Uno-X Mobility) is third in the standings (36 points). There are no categorised climbs on today’s route.

headline: White jersey
subtext: Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos) has been wearing the white jersey since stage 5 and is set to become the first British winner of the young riders standings of La Vuelta. He enters the final stage with a gap of 1’10’’ to Jakob Omrzel (Bahrain Victorious) and 17’24’’ to Léo Bisiaux (Decathlon CMA CGM).

headline: Team standings
subtext: Decathlon CMA CGM are set to win the team standings. XDS Astana are 39’01’’ behind the French team while Bahrain Victorious trail by 57’36’’.

headline: Combativity award
subtext: Tobias Johannessen (Uno-X Mobility) will race with a distinctive bib as he was named the most combative rider yesterday.

headline: La Vuelta 27 will start from Galicia
subtext: The Oficial Salida of the 82nd edition of La Vuelta will be set in Galicia, as announced before today’s stage by Javier Guillén, General Director of La Vuelta, and and Marcos Gómez, Commissioner of the Jacobean Holy Year. The race will begin with a linear stage in Santiago de Compostela. It will be the ninth time La Vuelta sets off from Galicia. It first happened in 1965 and, more recently, in 2016.

headline: Happy birthday Sepp, Nick, Thomas, Philippa…
subtext: Three riders celebrate their birthdays today at La Vuelta 26: - Sepp Kuss (Visma-Lease a Bike) turns 32 years old. He takes part in the Spanish Grand Tour for the 9th time consecutively. Three years ago, on his birthday, he was 3rd at Alto de l’Angliru, a result that proved instrumental en route to his overall victory a week later. Last year, he was 2nd at La Bola del Mundo on his birthday - Nick Schultz (NSN) also turns 32. This is his 6th participation in La Vuelta - Thomas Gloag (Pinarello Q36.5) turns 25 two days after finishing 3rd at Peñas Blancas. This is his first participation in La Vuelta Today is also the 68th birthday of Philippa York, formerly known as Robert Millar, 2nd of La Vuelta in 1985 and 1986.

headline: Farewell Steven, David, Pello, Magnus and Jesus
subtext: At the start, the organisers and the peloton celebrate five riders who are completing their final Grand Tour before retiring: - Steven Kruiswijk (Visma-Lease a Bike) - David de la Cruz (Pinarello Q36.5) - Pello Bilbao (Bahrain Victorious) - Magnus Cort (Uno-X Mobility) - Jesus Herrada (Burgos Burpellet BH)

headline: Let’s roll
subtext: The peloton make their way to the start proper with a 1.1 km parade.

headline: Stage 21 is ON!
subtext: The 142 riders who completed yesterday's stage are back in action. Movistar riders are in first line with a special jersey celebrating Enric Mas's achievements.

headline: Canal: "A dream come true"
subtext: To Carlos Canal, winning La Vuelta with Enric Mas is "a dream come true. We’ve all worked together to form a great team; we’ve been the best possible teammates and, with a leader like Enric, we’ve managed to dominate the second half of La Vuelta and win the race. He’s taken a huge step forward this year. For me, he’s been the best team leader we could have hoped for, and I hope he carries on like this and that we can enjoy watching him for many more years to come. Let’s hope we’re back on the start line next year; we can’t improve on Enric’s result, but we’ll fight to defend it.”

headline: The retiree’s words ahead of their final La Vuelta stage: "Joy and emotion"
subtext: Jesús Herrada (Burgos-Burpellet-BH): "Well, rather than sadness, it’s the emotion of looking back on all those years and all those moments: the good ones, the bad ones… It’s not sadness, it’s joy and emotion at all those moments that are coming to an end today. But anyway, this stage is over and a new one is beginning. There aren’t enough words to express my gratitude for the year I’ve had with [Burgos-Burpellet-BH]. They’ve treated me absolutely brilliantly, and honestly, I couldn’t have had a better final year. The ideal ending would have been a stage win. Today is our last chance. We know it’s very difficult, we’ve tried and we’ll definitely try again. So let’s enjoy it and give it our all." Pello Bilbao (Bahrain Victorious): "I’m excited. Up until now I’ve been more relaxed, more calm, holding back those emotions a little and focusing more on the day-to-day, on the race. But anyway, today I’m feeling more excited. Well, I’ve got to fight it out right to the end, in my own style, and not let this chance slip by. I’m raring to go. I know there’s a lot of accumulated fatigue, and today could also be a good chance to prove myself right to the end, to give it my all. And one of us – either me or Pau [Miquel] – I hope we’ll be in the fight for the stage win. I’ll carry on a bit further and we’ll say our goodbyes at Il Lombardia." Magnus Cort (Uno-X Mobility): "I think it will be very difficult, but I will definitely try to win today, and the team is there to support me. I think, if we would race from km 0 and from a breakaway, it would be a stage that would really suit me well, from a break. But I think, from the peloton, it will be more difficult for me. But I will do everything I can. I’ve always loved being in La Vuelta, and Spain in general, I’ve spent a big part of my career in Spain, so I want to say thank you to all the people of Spain for having me and being friendly my whole career. Spain has a special place in my heart, it’s my favourite country for racing, but also for training." David De La Cruz (Pinarello-Q36.5): "No, no [I’m not sad]. I certainly have a mix of emotions, obviously. Today is my last race as a professional cyclist; I’m finishing the season here at La Vuelta a España, my final season. Lots of emotions, but sadness is certainly not one of them. I’m finishing La Vuelta with injuries, but also with fond memories, not just of this Vuelta, but also of the other twelve I’ve taken part in. Gosh, I’m absolutely delighted and so grateful to have been able to live this dream. Yesterday, too, on the final climb, the Alguacil, I had the chance to savour the moment and feel the warmth of the crowds, which was something special and incredibly moving. So, I’m leaving with a full heart and feeling incredibly grateful." Steven Kruijswijk (Visma-Lease a Bike) spoke yesterday: "I have to say that [this Vuelta] is a special one. We've won seven stages with the team already. Hopefully we can add one more this weekend, but it's a really nice way of ending my career. I still had a good feeling on the bike, so I didn't have the feeling I couldn't support the team anymore. I did my job in the last few weeks, so I'm really grateful to be part of this team and to end it like this. And for sure, I always love this race. I had some good results myself as well. It's always really nice to race in Spain and I have good memories about it."

headline: Mas wins his first Grand Tour at 31 years old
subtext: Riders aged 30+ for their first Grand Tour victory (recent history): Enric Mas, 31, La Vuelta 2026 Geraint Thomas was 32 years old when he won the Tour de France 2018 Chris Horner, 41, La Vuelta 2013 Bradley Wiggins, 32, Tour de France 2012 Ryder Hesjedal, 31, Giro d’Italia 2012 Cadel Evans, 34, Tour de France 2011 Michel Scarponi, 31, Giro 2011 Carlos Sastre, 33, Tour de France 2008

headline: Riders aged 30+ for their first La Vuelta victory
subtext: Enric Mas, 31, La Vuelta 2026 Chris Horner, 41, La Vuelta 2013 Alexandre Vinokourov, 33, La Vuelta 2006 Tony Rominger, 31, La Vuelta 1992 Sean Kelly, 31, La Vuelta 1988 Joop Zoetemelk, 32, La Vuelta 1979 José Pesarrodona, 30, La Vuelta 1976 Agustin Tamames, 30, La Vuelta 1975 Ferdinand Bracke, 31, La Vuelta 1971 Jesus Loroño, 31, La Vuelta 1957 Angelo Conterno, 31, La Vuelta 1956 Zoetemelk went on to win the Tour de France in 1980, and Rominger won La Vuelta in 1993 and 1994 again before adding the Giro d’Italia to his record in 1995. The other riders in the list haven’t won another Grand Tour in their career.

subtext: So far, the peloton take it easy. It's time to celebrate having overcome the challenges of the last three weeks.

headline: Movistar increase the pace at the front of the peloton
subtext: The race is inside the final 90 kilometres.

headline: Landa: "I managed to turn my whole year around in a single day"
subtext: WInner yesterday at Collado del Alguacil, Mikel Landa (Soudal Quick-Step) is "still on cloud nine. Yesterday was a really exciting day and I managed to turn my whole year around in a single day. I think I needed something like this to move forward and approach the coming years in a different way, and yesterday was a great day. Hopefully we’ll be able to compete in La Vuelta next year [with Euskaltel-Euskadi]. It’s a tough battle to be among the top 30 teams and then secure an invitation, but we’ll give it our best shot."

headline: 24 kilometres in the first hour
subtext: After the early celebrations, the bunch have accelerated now.

headline: Elosegui: "We want to give it our all right up to the very last day"
subtext: Íñigo Elosegui and Kern Pharma raced aggressively to show their worth while the team searches a new sponsor for next year: "Juanjo [Oroz, the team manager] gave a moving speech, as always, reminding us of the team’s values, what it means to be part of this team and what we want to achieve in cycling. Although the project is going through a difficult period at the moment, we want to give it our all right up to the very last day and fight to win – that’s what’s in our DNA. This is what Juanjo has reminded us of: that we’ve always been like this and we’ll continue to be like this right up until the very last day. It’s a positive assessment. We wanted to win. So far it hasn’t been possible, we’ve still got one chance left, but we’ve been in the thick of it every single day: there was a second place for Urko [Berrade], fourth places, fifth places… this means we’ve been contesting the stage every single day, and winning is very, very difficult. But we’ve been close and we’ve fought for it as a team. Every rider has had their moment in the sun, so I think we can leave feeling happy."

headline: Carapaz: "I’m happy with what I’ve done"
subtext: Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost) will finish 4th overall after his many attacks en route to the Collado del Alguacil: “Yesterday was a good day for us. We knew we had a lot to play for, and although in the end it didn’t go quite as we’d hoped, we rode a fairly aggressive race, with those of us in contention for the podium staying in the mix. I’m leaving feeling happy. We gave it our all, we did something a bit different from the usual, and I gave everything I could to try and make it onto the podium. I’m happy with what I’ve done.”

headline: The final 70 kilometres of La Vuelta 26
subtext: The average speed since the start is up to almost 30 km/h, while it was below 15 km/h at the beginning of the stage.

headline: Romele: "I’m gonna suffer like the first days and will do my best"
subtext: Alessandro Romele (XDS Astana) discovered himself at La Vuelta 26 and aims fora final strong performance today: "Yes, actually, I was thinking [I may not finish] in the two easiest stages of this Vuelta, the first two stages of the third week. I don’t know what to say; it was maybe a virus, maybe not good recovery… Thanks to the doctor of the team, we managed, and here we are; last stage of the Vuelta, it’s a beautiful day. I spent 21 days in a super team, really good feelings, and we see today. It’s the last stage, I’m gonna suffer like the first days and will do my best. We can say it’s a new start, maybe a new chapter of y career. We’ll see what the end of the season will be like with this shape. Hopefully I can manage to do something good in the Italian classics, maybe Paris-Tours… We don’t know. First of all, a good recovery after the Vuelta, and then we’re gonna see."

headline: Van Aert: "This is way harder than Montmartre"
subtext: Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike) has been preparing stage 21 for quite a long time: “I saw it again this morning, but I did the climb already one time in February when I saw the course online. We were here for a camp in Sierra Nevada. It’s a rather long climb for the circuit. The climb is 2-km long and the circuit is only 10 k, so it will be a super hard repetition a 5-minute effort. I think the idea is similar [to the Montmartre circuit in the Tour] but honestly this is way harder.”

headline: Coquard: "Today is a bit of a mixed bag"
subtext: The winner of stage 8 in Xeraco, Bryan Coquard (Cofidis) hopes to be in the mix today: “It’s always special. For a start, it’s really great to finish a Grand Tour, especially when you’ve had some success in it. I’m really pleased to have won. I wanted to stay there to celebrate with my mates right up until the very last moment! And yes, today is a bit of a mixed bag. Let’s just say it’s going to be selective and tough. But we’ll do our very best to try and secure a good result. I think Van Aert will be able to attack. If there’s a small group behind him, Brennan will be there again.”

headline: The final 50 kilometres of La Vuelta 26
subtext: The peloton are about to enter Granada.

headline: The race is in Granada
subtext: The riders will pass the finish line a first time with 41.8 km to go. The road will rise immediately afterwards to climb to the Alhambra. The average speed after 2 hours: 32.3 km/h.

headline: First time at the finish line
subtext: 41.8km to go.

headline: The first climb to the Alhambra is done
subtext: Movistar set the pace on the ascent.

headline: Tronchon: "Van Aert can take a lot of risks"
subtext: After his victory in Elche de la Sierra (stage 10), Bastien Tronchon (Groupama-FDJ United) is a contender to double his tally in Granada: “It’s great to finish La Vuelta! There were a lot of riders who withdrew because of the heat we had in the middle of the race, so it’s already good that the eight of us are here at the finish, and it’s not quite over yet because there’s still a great stage to ride today. I’m feeling pretty good about it. I’ve tried to save as much energy as possible over the last two days, which were still very tough. It’s going to be a bit like the Champs-Élysées – a bit of chaos when it comes to positioning for the climb on the first few laps. Once the positioning is sorted, it’ll be a matter of legs, but first it’ll be important to get into a good position. I can’t say [that I know how to outmanoeuvre Van Aert] because he’s a great rider and a fine tactician, especially as there are two of them. Van Aert can take a lot of risks; he’ll know that Brennan is close behind. It’s not going to be easy to manage. But first and foremost, the main priority is positioning on the second climb, because normally Movistar should be controlling the race until the end of the first one.”

headline: 3 laps to go
subtext: The peloton just entered thefinal 30 kilometres with Groupama-FDJ United at the front.

headline: Paleni ups the ante on the second climb
subtext: Tronchon is on his wheel. The sprinters struggle at the back.

headline: Tronchon attacks
subtext: The first move of the day comes 28 kilometres from the line. He's followed by a dozen riders, starting with Johannessen and Brennan. Then it's Paret-Peintre, Fisher-Black...

headline: A small group of attackers with Tronchon, Nys, Romele...
subtext: Léo Bisiaux (Decathlon CMA CGM) joins Finn Fisher-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Matthew Brennan (Visma-Lease a Bike), Milan Vader (Pinarello Q36.5), Axel Laurance (Netcompany Ineos), Thibau Nys (Lidl-Trek), Bastien Tronchon (Groupama-FDJ United), Valentin Paret-Peintre (Soudal Quick-Step) and Alessandro Romele (XDS Astana). Santiago Buitrago (Bahrain Victorious) sets the pace 15 seconds behind with 22 kilometres remaining.

headline: 2 laps to go
subtext: Behind the leaders, the bunch has split in two parts. Uno-X Mobility drive the first peloton less than 10 seconds behind the leaders.

headline: The first chase group catch the leaders
subtext: Movistar set the pace behind them.

headline: 1 minute between the two bunches
subtext: The leaders are 17 km from the line.

headline: Lidl-Trek and Visma-Lease a Bike are the driving forces in the first group
subtext: Movistar pull the second bunch.

headline: The final lap!
subtext: Pau Miquel sets the pace for Pello Bilbao (Bahrain Victorious). The times for the overall standings are established now.

headline: Bilbao attacks, Van Aert is dropped!
subtext: 9 kilometres to go...

headline: Laurance counter-attacks
subtext: Over the top, Axel Laurance (Netcompany Ineos) passes Pello Bilbao (Bahrain Victorious). Matthew Brennan (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Bastien Tronchon (Groupama-FDJ United) struggle to keep up with the pace set by Alessandro Romele (XDS Astana) in pursuit.

headline: Laurance is caught by a small group
subtext: There are 11 riders at the frontwith 6.5 km to go.

headline: The final 5 kilometres of La Vuelta 26!
subtext: Laurance is here with Nys, Romele, Paret-Peintre, Bilbao, Widar... Brennan and Tronchon closed the gap.

headline: The leaders:
subtext: Brennan, Nys, Bilbao, Marti, Johannessen, Laurance, Tronchon, Paret-Peintre, Brenner, Romele, Debruyne and Widar are inside the last 3 kilometres.

headline: Last kilometre
subtext: Debruyne, Romele and Johannessen are opening a gap at the front.

headline: Tobias Johannessen wins stage 21 of La Vuelta 26!
subtext: The Norwegian takes his first Grand Tour stage ahead of Romele!

headline: Top 5
subtext: 1. Tobias Johannessen (Uno-X Mobility) 2. Alessandro Romele (XDS Astana) 3. Ramses Debruyne (Alpecin-Premier Tech) 4. Matthew Brennan (Visma-Lease a Bike) 5. Bastien Tronchon (Groupama-FDJ United)

headline: Enric Mas finishes and wins La Vuelta 26
subtext: A few metres behind the bunch, the Spaniard crosses the line with his six teammates by his side: Arcas, Aular, Canal, Castrillo, Garcia Pierna, and Romeo.
